content:
Dozens of declassified presidential briefing documents released Friday, on the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks, detail the intelligence gathered by government officials about Osama bin Laden and al-Qaeda before the hijackings that killed nearly 3,000 people and fundamentally reshaped America's national security landscape.

The documents show how intelligence analysts tracked bin Laden's movements and support networks, as well as concerns about possible attacks on U.S. targets. They also detail officials' understanding of his networks in the United States and other countries, including how his operations were funded.

CIA Director Ratcliffe described the move as an "act of extraordinary transparency," calling it the largest single declassification of presidential daily briefings by the agency. The President's Daily Brief is prepared by the intelligence community for top leaders and is highly classified.

The documents span from a February 1998 file titled "Terrorists Seek Weapons of Mass Destruction Capability" that mentioned bin Laden and other Islamic extremists — prepared for then-President Clinton — to a September 12, 2001, report noting that sources indicated the attacks had been planned for two years and that the U.S. Capitol was also among the targets.

An April 1998 document described the Taliban's unwillingness to hand over bin Laden, who was then seen as a "guest of honor" in Afghanistan, noting the Taliban were "grateful for his assistance during the Soviet occupation" and thus "unwilling to antagonize him by surveilling or restricting his activities."

In July 1998, briefers noted that "bin Laden may have prioritized attacking the United States on its own soil" and that he was "interested in conducting attacks with chemical and biological weapons."

Two months later, a briefer wrote that bin Laden's "preferred mode of attack was on the U.S. homeland in Washington" and that al-Qaeda "may fly an aircraft loaded with explosives into a U.S. city."

Potential hijackings were also discussed in December 1998, when a briefer described plotters who "had evaded security during a trial run at an undisclosed airport in New York" and that "elements of the bin Laden network had received training in hijacking."

Other documents detailed bin Laden's efforts to acquire materials for a "dirty bomb" — a conventional weapon laced with radioactive material. Intelligence officials said that by June 1999, his associates had conducted experiments with explosives to "enhance the energy output of the blast."

Roughly two years before the attacks, intelligence officials had picked up indications that bin Laden appeared to be concealing from the Taliban his true intent to launch unprovoked strikes against the United States. Briefings prepared for President George W. Bush in early 2001 focused in part on bin Laden's "rudimentary efforts to experiment with producing and deploying biological weapons."

A report one month before the attacks said bin Laden was "committed to launching terrorist attacks inside the United States" and noted that al-Qaeda's 1998 strikes on U.S. embassies "demonstrated that he was willing to spend years planning operations and would not be deterred by setbacks."

During August 2001, officials wrote that "suspicious activity in this country consistent with preparations for hijackings or other types of attacks has been observed, including recent surveillance of federal buildings in New York," adding that the FBI was "conducting approximately 70 full-field investigations nationwide that it considers related to bin Laden."

Many of the documents are redacted to hide the names of sources and other identifying information. The documents do not appear to yield significant new breakthroughs about the plot itself or U.S. officials' understanding of the events as they unfolded.

In the years after the attacks, a bipartisan commission pointed to a lack of intelligence sharing between agencies such as the CIA and FBI and issued recommendations that led to the creation of new posts, including the director of national intelligence to oversee the intelligence community and the National Counterterrorism Center, which analyzes terrorism information at home and abroad and operates across government departments.

Asked about the declassified documents, the White House pointed to another set of files the National Archives also declassified on Friday. Those include transcripts of interviews conducted with national security officials from the Clinton and Bush administrations by the commission that investigated the attacks from 2002 to 2004.
